claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced plastic strain relative to pure tungsten at high service temperatures.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced toughness relative to pure tungsten at high service temperatures.
Lattice distortion arising from the multielement composition governs the alloy's enhanced plastic strain and toughness.
Grain-boundary stabilization arising from the multielement composition governs the alloy's enhanced plastic strain and toughness.
Lattice distortion and grain-boundary stabilization promote more homogeneous dislocation activity than in pure tungsten.
Lattice distortion and grain-boundary stabilization delay crack initiation relative to pure tungsten.
The modified material is an equimolar alloy of W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr.
Producing both materials by matched powder metallurgy, sintering, and heat treatment can provide comparable grain sizes and minimal processing-induced defects.
Introducing equimolar Ta, Ti, V, and Zr into the tungsten-based material induces distinctive lattice distortions.
The multielement intervention can produce grain-boundary segregation.
Grain-boundary segregation or precipitation improves dislocation mobility.
Grain-boundary segregation or precipitation improves grain-boundary cohesion.
Severe lattice distortions activate additional dislocation slip systems.
Minor segregation or finely dispersed precipitates stabilize grain boundaries.
The proposed dual mechanism distributes plastic deformation more uniformly.
The proposed dual mechanism promotes effective crack-tip blunting.
At high temperature, WTaTiVZr will have greater strain-to-failure than matched pure tungsten.
At high temperature, WTaTiVZr will have greater fracture toughness than matched pure tungsten.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate at service-relevant temperatures of at least 1200°C and at plasma-facing-component-relevant strain rates.
The proposed effects may be less pronounced at substantially lower temperatures or under extreme loading rates.
